rows.description: I am proud to be different and refuse to fit in. Wise: enjoy it while remaining open to others. Harmful: using superiority as armour against connection.
I use charm and gossip to climb the social ladder. It works, and I feel hollow. Wise: recognise the cost to trust and choose honest ways to belong.
I am popular and sense envy behind compliments. Wise: stay kind and honest, do not assume all attention is friendship, and keep close a few real friends. Harmful: cruelty to stay on top.
I am mocked as weird or poor or fat. It is unfair and not my fault. Wise: protect my self-respect, find spaces where I fit, and report harassment. Harmful: believing their story.
Feels devotion, wonder and belonging while participating; faith is absorbed through stories, music and ritual before argument.
I thank God for my family and food before eating. The feeling is warm and simple. Gratitude can also become action, like sharing my food with someone who has less.
At the gathering I am told I cannot join because of who I am. It hurts and confuses me. It is not my fault; I can tell a trusted adult and know that real faith does not shut a child out.
I listen to the religious teacher's stories and believe them fully. Trust is natural at this age; over time I learn to notice whether teachings promote kindness and never fear, cruelty or secrecy.
Confuses jealousy and monitoring with love; learns to spot control, isolation and guilt-tripping as warning signs.
Feels shattered and embarrassed after a "no"; healing comes from time, support and remembering that rejection is not a verdict of worth.

I see my crush as flawless and hang on every word. It feels wonderful and blinds me. Wise: enjoy the feeling, remember they are an ordinary person, and keep my own life going. Harmful: rebuilding myself for them.
Idealizes the person and checks their profile constantly; reality check comes from talking with friends and noticing their actual behaviour.
My parents sigh over my marks and compare me to a cousin. I feel small. It is not my fault they are anxious; I can say I will try harder and ask for help without losing my self-respect.
My parents beam and tell everyone about my marks. I feel happy but also pressure to do it again. It helps to enjoy their joy while remembering that my worth is more than my rank.
I got fewer marks than I hoped and think I am stupid. One result is not a verdict on me; a wiser view asks which topics went wrong and how to practise them.
My friend topped the class and I feel a sting in my stomach. It is normal; asking what helped him study turns envy into learning, while running him down only hurts us both.
I see my ex happy with someone new and feel a stab of jealousy. I let the feeling pass without stalking their profile, remember my own reasons for leaving, and put attention into building my life.

I compare my current partner with my ex and feel dissatisfied. I see that memory is edited and that I am comparing a real person with a highlight reel; I appreciate present strengths and speak honestly about needs.
Years later I feel ready to forgive an ex. I release resentment for my own peace and can say so briefly if it helps, without reopening the relationship or needing their apology first.
I still feel angry at how an ex treated me. I acknowledge the wrong, seek support from friends or a counsellor, and avoid revenge posts or messages; carrying rage keeps me tied to them.
My grandmother died and the house feels empty. I miss her stories and her hands. Grief comes in waves; letting myself cry and remember her is a way of loving her still.
I do not understand where my grandfather has gone and adults give different answers. It is okay to ask questions and to hear that people have different beliefs and that nobody knows everything.
Relatives gather for prayers and rituals after the death. The songs and food give me a sense of belonging. Whatever our beliefs, rituals help families carry sorrow together.
